questions.question: Why must permission enforcement happen at retrieval rather than at the UI?
options: The generator will summarize and thereby leak whatever enters its context
The interface cannot reliably hide the citation chips once an answer renders
Retrieval runs before page render, so the same filter is cheaper there
Users can switch off a client-side filter from their browser console

questions.question: What does every chunk carry at ingest for ACL-aware retrieval?
options: A tenant-specific encryption key the gateway presents in order to read it
The owner's role, used to rank internal results above the public ones
An ACL payload naming the users, groups, or roles allowed to see it
A signed hash of the source document, re-checked before it is returned

questions.question: Ninety percent of the corpus is forbidden to a user. What happens when the pipeline post-filters an ANN top-100?
options: About ninety candidates survive, because the filter runs before scoring
About ten candidates survive, and the answers come out thin as a result
The index rebalances its partitions so eligible documents rank higher
The reranker restores depth by scoring the discarded candidates again

questions.question: Why is post-filter starvation also a security issue, not just a quality issue?
options: It slows legitimate queries enough to invite denial-of-service abuse
It raises the embedding bill, crowding out spending on audit logging
It forces nightly re-indexing, during which the filter is not applied
Shifting result counts let a prober infer that hidden documents exist

questions.question: Why resolve group membership at query time rather than denormalizing it into documents?
options: A query-time lookup is faster than reading a group field off each chunk
Membership changes then take effect without re-indexing the documents
Documents stay small enough to fit the embedding model's input cap
Group names are high-cardinality, so an inverted index cannot hold them

questions.question: A document's ACL is tightened at 14:00. What must happen beyond the metadata update?
options: The document must be re-embedded, since its vector encodes its audience
The whole index generation must be rebuilt before the change takes hold
Cached retrievals and answers derived from that document must be purged
Every active session must re-authenticate to pick up the new group list

questions.question: Which isolation option is the weakest?
options: A separate retrieval cluster provisioned for each paying tenant
A separate index per tenant, all hosted inside one shared cluster
One shared index divided into a namespace or partition per tenant
One shared index with tenant_id applied as an ordinary query filter

questions.question: An answer cache is keyed by query text alone. What can happen?
options: Tenant A is served the answer that was cached for tenant B's query
Cache entries expire on first write, so the hit rate stays near zero
Queries bypass the retriever, so the citations point at wrong chunks
Vectors from two tenants collide and silently overwrite one another

questions.question: What does the response layer add when the retrieval filter is already mandatory?
options: It renders each answer faster by reusing the tenant's cached template
It scores embedding quality so a drifting tenant can be re-embedded
It re-verifies each document's tenant tag, catching a buggy filter
It rate-limits traffic so one tenant's spike cannot starve the rest

questions.question: Where should tenant context come from on every request?
options: A tenant parameter supplied by the client on each API call it makes
The authenticated session, injected by the gateway into the filter
The tenant tag stored on whichever documents the retriever returns
A signed cookie the browser sets when the user picks a workspace

questions.question: A shared query rewriter is fine-tuned on all tenants' query logs. What is the risk?
options: The rewriter's added latency is charged to every tenant equally
The training logs eventually outgrow the model's own context window
The rewriter forgets the earliest tenants as newer data dominates it
One tenant's phrasing can be regurgitated into another's session

questions.question: Why is tenant_id made a first-class schema field from day one?
options: Retrofitting it into a shared index means a full rebuild plus an incident
A declared tenant field is what lets the vector store skip ACL resolution
A declared tenant field is required before per-tenant encryption keys work
Filters over undeclared fields fall back to post-filtering, which starves

questions.question: What is indirect prompt injection?
options: An attacker repeatedly queries the model to extract its system prompt
An attacker fine-tunes the embedding model on poisoned training pairs
Adversarial instructions planted in content the retriever later fetches
An attacker edits the system prompt through a misconfigured admin page

questions.question: Why does retrieval make prompt injection precise?
options: Retrieval strips provenance markers, so the payload arrives looking trusted
The pipeline delivers the payload exactly when it is most relevant
The reranker promotes instruction-like text above ordinary prose
Retrieved text skips the tokenizer, so no filter ever inspects it

questions.question: Which output pattern suggests an exfiltration attempt via injection?
options: An answer formatted as bullet points when prose had been requested
An answer written in unusually short sentences with no citations
An answer citing many more sources than the question really needed
A rendered link whose URL carries conversation data in its query string

questions.question: What is the structural defense against a compromised reader model?
options: The reader holds no tools or credentials, and an orchestrator reads its output
The reader is retrained weekly on the newest injection payloads observed
The reader runs with a smaller context window so payloads cannot fit in
The orchestrator rewrites every user query before the reader ever sees it

questions.question: What is the correct security posture toward prompt injection as of early 2026?
options: Ingest-time sanitization catches the patterns, so the risk is closed
Provenance tags on retrieved text remove the risk once they are applied
Assume some injection succeeds and limit what a success can reach
Admit only curated first-party documents, which cannot be poisoned

questions.question: What does a per-tenant canary document detect?
options: Background indexing jobs that have fallen behind the live corpus
Its unique string surfacing inside another tenant's answer
An embedding model version change that shifted every vector
A judge model that prefers outputs from its own model family
